issues.item: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, these items are hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. 'Story Feels Unreal' and especially 'Overwhelm on Recall' imply a disjointed, emotionally intense trauma memory, which fits the strong Memory↔Threat links. In contrast, 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily' suggests unusually easy narrative access to the trauma and directly pulls against the other memory items. For a severe PTSD profile centered on intrusive, overwhelming childhood domestic violence memories, this Memory combination is clinically inconsistent.

issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, these two items directly contradict each other: being able to talk about the trauma very easily is incompatible with simultaneously being unable to put the event into words. This is a clear within-node inconsistency.

vignette:
Mariam is a 30-year-old Middle Eastern American woman who came to treatment after years of living as though danger could break through at any moment. She is divorced and works nights as a bartender, a job she chose partly because the space behind the bar feels defined and contained. She can keep her back near the shelves, know where the exits are, and watch the room without having to stand exposed in the middle of it. Open spaces trouble her. Crossing a wide parking lot after a shift, or stepping out onto an empty sidewalk before dawn, leaves her feeling visible and unprotected in a way she struggles to explain.

The event she returns to is from childhood, when she witnessed domestic violence in her home. What remains most vivid is not a story she tells in sequence but a set of fragments that arrive with force: the sound of a door slamming hard enough to shake the frame, her father's body moving suddenly across the room, her mother stepping back, the speed with which an ordinary evening became dangerous. She remembers watching movements before she understood words, learning to read the lift of an arm, the turn of a shoulder, the change in pace across a room. Even now, those moments feel stored in her body more than in language. When she tries to describe what happened, she often stops mid-sentence and says she knows exactly what happened but cannot find the words. If she pushes herself to continue, she becomes flooded and has to stop altogether, ashamed and frustrated that something so central in her life still seems unspeakable.

In the years after, Mariam came to believe that people cannot be trusted, especially when they seem calm. Her mistrust is not abstract; it lives in constant small calculations. She watches for sudden movements from customers leaning over the bar, from men reaching quickly into their pockets, from strangers shifting sharply in line at the liquor distributor. Her body goes on immediate alert before she has fully registered why. At work she is known as composed and efficient, but beneath that control she tracks who is entering, who is drinking too fast, who might become unpredictable. If a patron raises an arm too quickly to wave her down, she flinches internally and then covers it, tightening her face and forcing herself into an even tone.

She tries hard to control her emotions and rarely lets herself cry, shake, or visibly lose composure. It matters intensely to her not to come undone in front of anyone. She has come to doubt her own judgment and says she cannot rely on herself to do the right thing when it counts. That self-doubt appears in ordinary decisions as much as in emergencies. Before leaving home, she checks the locks and windows repeatedly, then doubts whether she checked correctly and circles back again. At night, once she is in bed, she often gets up to confirm the front door is locked one more time. She tells herself this is the only way to be prepared.

Preparation occupies much of her thinking. On her drive to work, she mentally rehearses worst-case scenarios: a fight breaking out at the bar, someone following her to her car, an intruder getting into her apartment, a man misreading a brief interaction and becoming aggressive. She runs through what she would do, where she would stand, what she could grab, how she would get out. She experiences this as necessary rather than excessive; without rehearsing, she feels foolish and exposed. Still, the habit leaves little room for rest. By the time a shift begins, she is already tense.

Over time her life has narrowed around a small set of places that feel tolerable: behind the bar, in her apartment after the locks are checked, and in a few familiar corners of her routine. Elsewhere she feels unsteady. During busy service, coworkers sometimes ask her to cross the floor to clear tables or help on the patio, and she dislikes the open layout there, feeling too visible and too far from cover. Her divorce sits in this same landscape of mistrust and self-doubt. She does not offer a simple explanation for it, only that living closely with another person never felt truly safe and that she was always bracing, second-guessing herself, and waiting for a shift she might miss.

What brought her to seek help was not one new crisis but exhaustion. After a recent shift, a customer made a sudden movement while arguing with someone beside him, and Mariam found herself so intensely on guard that she had to step into the stockroom and stand still until the surge passed. Later, alone in her apartment, she checked the locks again and again and realized she no longer knew what "enough" would feel like. She came in saying she is tired of living inside constant readiness. What frightens her most is the possibility that she will never be able to trust anyone, including herself. What she hopes for, cautiously, is to feel safe in more than a few narrow places and to speak about what she witnessed without becoming overwhelmed or losing control.
